newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mixed, gold down, PGMs up.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mixed, gold down, PGMs up.

text.p: COMEX gold and silver prices ended lower Monday, giving back some of Friday's gains, but NYMEX platinum group metal (PGM) futures ended higher, with Russian supplies still in doubt.

"There wasn't any follow through in gold after the recovery on Thursday and Friday last week, and everybody's expecting the August/December spread to get crushed this week as the rollover continues, and sentiment remains bearish," FIMAT New York trader John Tyree said.
COMEX August gold ended down $3.40 at $326.20 an ounce, following a run up to 11 day highs at $330.90 Friday.
The August/December spread ended around $3.40 an ounce, after widening out to $3.70 Friday, but has been narrowing steadily since late May when it was around $5.60 an ounce.

After the recovery in the August gold contract late last week, momentum oscillators, such as a regular nine-day relative strength indicator (RSI) are back to the neutral 50 percent level, suggesting there is now room for more downside, analysts said.
The contract's five-day moving-average remains below its 21-day average, which in turn, remains well below the 55-day average, suggesting the downtrend remains intact also.
The latest CFTC Commitments of Traders data, released late Friday, showed funds held record net short positions of 74,588 COMEX gold contracts as of July 15.

But, after climbing to its highest levels in 18 months in recent weeks, COMEX gold open interest fell 5,107 lots Friday to 213,895 contracts, suggesting last week's action was mostly short covering, rather than accumulation by investors.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted around $325.30/80, compared to the London Monday afternoon fix at $326.20, and the New York close Friday at $328.70/20.

Gold fixed at a 12 year low early this month at $315.75 in London, in the wake of news of a sale of 167 tonnes of gold by the Australian central bank, which encouraged massive amounts of extra short selling by hedge funds.

Implied lease rates for gold eased further to around 2.08 percent for one month Monday, from a six month high around 2.60 percent last week, suggesting hedge fund borrowing demand is continuing to ease, traders said.
"Gold prices, in our strongly held opinion, are moving sideways-to-lower for many months to come," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said.
"Rallies will increasingly be seen as forward selling opportunities by producers, funds, dealers, and central banks."
COMEX September silver ended down 1.2 cents at $4.258 an ounce, while the September/December spread narrowed further to 5.7 cents an ounce.

"Although we continue to expect that sub-$5.00 silver prices will attract strong demand from the U.S., Japan and India, the lack of investor demand for hard assets, combined with the weight of selling from investment funds, could pressure silver prices to still lower levels, especially if gold prices weaken further," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.

"We see the potential for a test of the $4.00 area, where some price stability should materialize, reflecting prospects for a continuation of the long-term shortfall between world production and consumption of silver, and the resulting drawdown in stocks."
Meanwhile, NYMEX October platinum ended up 20 cents at $399.50 an ounce, after climbing back over $400.00 Friday, for the first time in two weeks.
NYMEX September palladium gained $4.95 to end at $171.30.

Russian shipments of palladium to Japan resumed last week, with the arrival of palladium at Narita Airport in Tokyo, but no platinum arrivals have yet been reported, and no spot deals with the Russians have been concluded either, traders said.
"We understand from some market sources that a fresh squeeze is looming in palladium and, to a lesser extent, platinum at the end of this month," Merrill Lynch's Arnold said.
